column5: CEOs received substantial rents, partly because pay is set by negotiation and with weak oversight. But bad CEO can do huge damage to a firm.
column8: Yes, but not sufficient given that disperse shareholders may not have sufficient incentives to monitor performance.
I weakly disagree. I suspect that this requirement is ineffective -- so it silences some critics without solving any agency problems.

column5: I am fairly confident that the literature is not conclusive on this for the "typical" CEO.
column8: I don't think this policy will do much though their have been a few high profile institution-led No votes on these resolutions.
I don't know if it affected pay, but shareholders should have the right to express some view on this.
Seems to have had little effect so far.  Gives stockholders potentially more power at probably low costs of administering it.

column5: Big discrepancy between  CEO compensation and long-term shareholder returns.
column8: "Non-binding" means the mandate has no teeth

column5: There are reasons to believe CEO wages = marginal product & to think they are paid more, but I'm unaware of any credible empirical evidence
column8: Difficult to see harm but there is plenty of evidence that more sunshine can improve firm performance.  See below link for an example
Ex ante, giving management a significant stake in a company has its logic, so cutting the payoff ex post may be a problem.

column5: Very hard to measure MP of CEO. Harder still to assess MP of alternatives to CEO. So CEO mkt not competitive in normal sense.
column8: Direct shareholder intervention has benefits as well as costs. Costs much underappreciated in current climate. Still, some oversight needed.

column5: This depends on how the CEO adds value--as a % increase on the firm's profit base or as an absolute amt.  If the former, no is more likely.
column8: The vote is good for governance, but mandating it is not. If you don't like how executives are paid, sell the shares.

column5: Commonly asserted but it is very hard to tell.  The fact that CEO pay fell during the 2000s is not widely known.
column8: We know that it does not seemed to have changed outcomes much so far.  Does take up some resources, but the threat might wind up being ok.

column5: Obviously, there are abuses, but the exec. market is reasonably competitive.  Some contribute far more to shareholder value than their pay.
column8: Mandates are not necessary.  Potential shareholders do not have to own shares in companies whose corp gov is not to their liking.

column5: I do not know enough about the empirical evidence to weigh in.
column8: Sounds like a good idea in theory, but I do not know enough about implementation to weigh in.

column5: US CEO current pay much higher than in other countries and than in the past suggesting over-pricing
column8: Unlikely to have a strong impact

column5: While trends in CEO pay may suggest this, I know of no hard evidence, particularly none that bears on the "typical" US corporation.
column8: It is hard to see how a non-binding vote by generally uninformed shareholders is likely to have benefits exceeding its coss.

column5: 2 Reasons: 1. Winner's curse. 2 asymetric payoffs (CEO wins when things go well and does not suffer when things go sour. Combo = overpay.
column8: More transparency is good.  Better would be to require disclosure of the process consultants use to set pay. Benchmarking is anit market.

column5: If you had asked the question the other way (we know that they are paid their marginal valuation) I would have strongly diagreed.
column8: The cost is minimal, while the benefit of transparency and societal pressure against excesses high.
